tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: A debate differs from a quarrel in that a debate is:
options: A structured, rule-governed exchange of arguments on a motion, while a quarrel is an emotional dispute
questions.explanation: A discussion is open and cooperative; a debate is competitive.

questions.question_text: A motion in a debate is:
options: The statement or proposition being debated, e.g., "This House believes that cash should be abolished"
questions.explanation: The two sides argue for and against it.

questions.question_text: The types of motions include:
questions.explanation: E.g., "THW ban single-use plastics" is a policy motion.

questions.question_text: THB, THW and THR stand for:
options: This House Believes, This House Would, This House Regrets

questions.question_text: The proposition (government) and the opposition respectively:
options: Support the motion and argue against it

questions.question_text: The burden of proof in a debate lies mainly on:
options: The proposition, which must prove the motion
questions.explanation: The opposition may simply disprove it.

questions.question_text: Defining the motion is important because:
options: It sets the scope of the debate and avoids misunderstandings

questions.question_text: Debating as a rhetorical strategy means:
options: Using structured argument and persuasion to convince an audience

questions.question_text: A benefit of debating is:
options: Improved critical thinking, communication and confidence

questions.question_text: The British Parliamentary format has:
options: Four teams of two speakers each: Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government and Closing Opposition

questions.question_text: Roles in a parliamentary debate include:
options: Prime Minister, Deputy PM, Leader of Opposition, Members and Whips
questions.explanation: Each speaker has a defined task.

questions.question_text: The Asian Parliamentary format has:
options: Two teams of three speakers (PM, Deputy PM and Government Whip versus the opposition), plus reply speeches
questions.explanation: Reply speeches are given by the first or second speaker.

questions.question_text: The Oxford-style debate is:
options: A formal debate in which the audience votes before and after to decide the winner by the shift in opinion
questions.explanation: It is popular for public debates.

questions.question_text: The Lincoln–Douglas format is:
options: A one-on-one debate focused on values and ethics
questions.explanation: It is common in US schools.

questions.question_text: Policy debate is:
options: A team debate (two per team) focused on a policy proposal, with heavy use of evidence

questions.question_text: The Karl Popper format has:
options: Two teams of three with cross-examination between speeches

questions.question_text: The World Schools style has:
options: Teams of three speakers with a reply speech, mixing prepared and impromptu motions
questions.explanation: It is used at international school competitions.

questions.question_text: Compared with the Lincoln–Douglas format, British Parliamentary debate is:
options: A team format with four teams, while LD is one-on-one
questions.explanation: Formats differ in teams and style.

questions.question_text: The structure of a debating speech is:
options: Introduction, signposting, arguments with rebuttal, and conclusion
questions.explanation: It should be clear and timed.

questions.question_text: The Toulmin model of argument consists of:
options: Claim, grounds (data), warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal
questions.explanation: It is a framework for analysing arguments.

questions.question_text: In the Toulmin model, the claim, grounds and warrant are respectively:
options: The assertion; the evidence; the link between evidence and claim
The evidence; the claim; the link
The link; the claim; the evidence
The assertion; the link; the evidence
questions.explanation: E.g., claim: ban plastics; grounds: pollution data; warrant: pollution is harmful.

questions.question_text: PEEL stands for:
Types of evidence in a debate include:
options: Statistics, expert opinion, examples and case studies
questions.explanation: Evidence should be relevant and credible.

questions.question_text: To build a case for a motion, you should:
options: Define the motion, set a framework and develop 2–3 strong arguments with evidence

questions.question_text: A framework (or model) in a debate is:
options: A set of criteria or a plan that defines how the debate should be judged or how the proposition will operate

tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: To prepare 2–3 strong arguments, you should:
options: Choose distinct, well-evidenced points that support the motion

questions.question_text: Rebuttal is:
options: Responding to and refuting the opponent's arguments, by identifying the argument, stating the response, giving evidence and showing the impact

questions.question_text: Rebuttal techniques include:
options: Denying the premise, showing irrelevance, providing counter-evidence, showing the argument is weak and turning it

questions.question_text: "Turning" an argument means:
options: Showing that the opponent's argument actually supports your side
questions.explanation: It is a powerful form of rebuttal.

questions.question_text: A Point of Information (POI) is:
options: A short question or remark offered to the speaker during their speech, which they may accept or decline
questions.explanation: It is offered politely by standing and saying "On that point, sir/madam."

questions.question_text: A speaker should accept:
options: About one or two POIs per speech, to show confidence and engagement
questions.explanation: They should decline politely if disruptive.

questions.question_text: Flowing is:
options: Taking structured notes of all arguments and rebuttals during a debate
questions.explanation: It helps in rebuttal and judging.

questions.question_text: Adjudication criteria in a debate include:
Matter, manner and method refer to:
options: What is said, how it is said and how it is organised
questions.explanation: They are the basis of scoring.

questions.question_text: The best opening for a one-minute proposition speech on "Social media does more harm than good" is:
options: "Social media harms mental health, spreads misinformation and wastes time, and today I will prove its harms outweigh its benefits."
questions.explanation: It states the position and arguments.

questions.question_text: The best opening for an opposition speech on the same motion is:
options: "This motion is wrong because I say so."
"Social media connects people, creates opportunities and spreads information; its benefits outweigh its harms."
questions.explanation: It takes the opposite stance with reasons.

questions.question_text: The best opening for a proposition speech on "Cash should be abolished" is:
options: "Abolishing cash would reduce crime, tax evasion and corruption while making transactions faster."
questions.explanation: It states a claim and reasons.

questions.question_text: The best opening for an opposition speech on "Cash should be abolished" is:
options: "Abolishing cash would exclude the poor and the elderly and fail when technology breaks."

questions.question_text: A good rebuttal to "Online education cannot replace classroom teaching" is:
options: "Online education offers flexibility, wider access and interactive tools, and studies show comparable outcomes."

questions.question_text: A good rebuttal to "Artificial intelligence will take away all jobs" is:
options: "AI automates tasks but also creates new jobs and roles, as earlier technologies did."
questions.explanation: It counters with a historical argument.

questions.question_text: An argument for "This House would ban single-use plastics" is:
options: They pollute oceans and harm wildlife
questions.explanation: Other arguments: waste burden, health effects.

questions.question_text: An argument against "This House would ban single-use plastics" is:
options: A ban can hurt small businesses and substitutes may have their own environmental costs

questions.question_text: A good opening for a debate on "Remote work should be the default" is:
options: "Good evening. Today we will show that remote work increases productivity and widens opportunities."
questions.explanation: It greets and states the stance.

questions.question_text: A strong case for "Financial literacy should be compulsory in schools" is that:
options: It prepares students to manage money, avoid debt and plan for the future

questions.question_text: A strong case against "Financial literacy should be compulsory in schools" is that:
options: The curriculum is already crowded, and it may be better taught by families or as an elective

questions.question_text: A moderator is:
options: A neutral person who manages the debate, enforces rules and keeps the discussion fair

questions.question_text: Before the debate, a moderator should:
options: Understand the motion and format, brief the speakers and confirm time rules

questions.question_text: A moderator should open a debate by:
options: Welcoming the audience, introducing the motion and speakers, and explaining the rules

questions.question_text: A moderator manages time by:
options: Keeping strict time limits with signals or a timekeeper

questions.question_text: When a speaker exceeds time, the moderator should:
options: Politely but firmly signal and ask them to conclude

tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: When there are personal attacks, the moderator should:
options: Intervene calmly, remind speakers to address arguments and not people

questions.question_text: A moderator maintains neutrality by:
options: Avoiding personal opinions and treating both sides equally

questions.question_text: When the audience disrupts, the moderator should:
The audience Q&A should be conducted by:
options: Inviting brief, relevant questions, allocating time fairly and directing them to speakers

questions.question_text: A moderator should close a debate by:
options: Thanking the speakers and audience, summarising neutrally and announcing the result procedure

questions.question_text: Qualities of a good moderator include:
options: Neutrality, fairness, authority with politeness and time sense
questions.explanation: Active listening and tact help too.

questions.question_text: A challenge a moderator faces is:
options: Dominant speakers or heated exchanges, handled with firm, polite control

questions.question_text: A good opening script for a moderator introducing a debate on "Cashless economy" is:
options: "Good afternoon, everyone. Today's motion is 'This House believes India should become a cashless economy.' Let us welcome our speakers."

questions.question_text: A good closing script for a moderator is:
options: "Thank you to our speakers and audience for a thoughtful debate. The adjudicators will now announce the result."

questions.question_text: Moderating an online debate differs in that:
options: The moderator must also manage technology, muting and chat, and keep equal speaking time

questions.question_text: Ethics of debating include:
options: Honesty, respect, fair use of evidence and attacking arguments not people

questions.question_text: One should attack arguments and not people because:
options: Personal attacks are irrelevant (ad hominem) and unfair

questions.question_text: Honesty is important in debating, and sources should be:
Cherry-picking evidence is:
options: Selecting only evidence that supports your side while ignoring contrary evidence

questions.question_text: A "gish gallop" is:
options: Overwhelming an opponent with many rapid, weak arguments so they cannot respond to all

questions.question_text: Unethical debating tactics include:
options: Misrepresenting evidence, insulting and deliberately wasting time

questions.question_text: To accept a result gracefully, one should:
options: Congratulate the winners and learn from feedback

questions.question_text: The ethical use of emotion in debating is to:
options: Support arguments with honest emotion without manipulating the audience

questions.question_text: Debating promotes democracy and free speech by:
options: Encouraging open exchange of views and respect for differing opinions

questions.question_text: Both-side-ism is:
options: Presenting two sides as equally valid even when evidence strongly favours one (false balance)

questions.question_text: An example of false balance in media is:
options: Giving equal airtime to a climate scientist and a climate denier as though evidence is equal
questions.explanation: It creates the impression of a 50–50 debate.

questions.question_text: Both-side-ism is problematic because:
options: It misrepresents the weight of evidence and can spread misinformation
questions.explanation: Not all views are equally supported.

questions.question_text: The media can avoid both-side-ism by:
options: Giving equal time to every view
Weighing evidence, labelling claims accurately and not giving equal weight to unsupported views

questions.question_text: Debating both sides of a motion differs from both-side-ism in that debating:
options: Is a training exercise with assigned sides, not a claim that both sides are equally true

questions.question_text: The fallacy of relativism is:
options: Claiming that all views are equally valid because truth depends on the person or culture

tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: An example of subjective relativism is:
options: "That's true for you, but not for me," about a factual claim
questions.explanation: It denies shared standards of truth.

questions.question_text: The claim "all truth is relative" is self-defeating because:
options: If it is true, then it is itself only relative and cannot be universally true

questions.question_text: Tolerance of persons differs from acceptance of all ideas in that one can:
options: Respect people while still criticising their ideas

questions.question_text: Cultural relativism is:
options: The view that all cultures are the same
The view that a culture's practices should be understood within its own context; it becomes a fallacy when it excuses harmful practices from criticism
questions.explanation: Understanding is not the same as endorsement.

questions.question_text: The principle of charity is:
options: Interpreting it in its weakest form
Interpreting an opponent's argument in its strongest, most reasonable form before responding

questions.question_text: Philosophers associated with the principle of charity include:
options: Donald Davidson and W.V. Quine (and Neil Wilson)
questions.explanation: It is used in interpreting speech and arguments.

questions.question_text: Steel-manning is:
options: Restating an opponent's argument in its strongest form before rebutting it
questions.explanation: It is the opposite of straw-manning.

questions.question_text: Rapoport's rules (popularised by Daniel Dennett) say that you should first:
options: Re-express the opponent's position so clearly that they say "I wish I'd put it that way", then list agreements, mention what you learned, and only then rebut

questions.question_text: The principle of charity differs from the straw man fallacy in that charity:
options: Strengthens the opponent's argument before responding, while the straw man weakens or distorts it

questions.question_text: A benefit of the principle of charity in debates is that it:
options: Promotes fair, productive and respectful debate and reveals real points of disagreement

questions.question_text: A limit of the principle of charity is that it:
options: Does not require accepting obviously bad faith, nonsense or hateful arguments
questions.explanation: One should still criticise weak arguments.

questions.question_text: The strongest charitable restatement of "Taxes are theft" is:
options: "Taxation involves taking resources without individual consent, so it needs strong justification and limits."

questions.question_text: The strongest charitable restatement of "Remote work kills creativity" is:
options: "Face-to-face interaction may spark spontaneous idea sharing that remote work can reduce."

questions.question_text: "All opinions on climate change deserve equal airtime" is an example of:
questions.explanation: It ignores the weight of evidence.

questions.question_text: "Who are you to say my culture is wrong? It's all relative" is an example of:
The principle of charity differs from both-side-ism and relativism in that it:
options: Concerns the quality of interpreting arguments, not treating all views as equal

questions.question_text: In a short debate on "Cashless payments are better than cash," a charitable rebuttal would begin:
options: "I understand your concern about those without digital access; however, UPI inclusion programmes are narrowing that gap."

questions.question_text: These concepts improve workplace discussions by:
options: Encouraging respectful listening, evidence-based arguments and better decisions

questions.question_text: A good opening for a proposition speech on "Online education is better than classroom education" is:
options: "Online education offers flexibility, affordability and wider access, making it better than classroom education."
questions.explanation: It states the stance and reasons.

questions.question_text: A good opening for an opposition speech on the same motion is:
options: "Classroom education offers interaction, discipline and hands-on learning that online education cannot match."

questions.question_text: A good rebuttal to "If we allow remote work, productivity will fall" is:
options: "Studies show remote workers are often as productive or more, with fewer commute-related losses."

questions.question_text: The role of the timekeeper in a debate is to:
options: Track speaking time and signal speakers when time is nearly up or over
questions.explanation: They knock or show cards at set times.

questions.question_text: The role of the Whip in a parliamentary debate is to:
options: Summarise the team's case and respond to the opposition's main points without introducing new arguments
questions.explanation: The Whip speech closes the team's case.

questions.question_text: A definitional challenge is:
options: Disputing the proposition's definition of the motion as unfair or unreasonable
questions.explanation: It is used when a definition is too narrow.

questions.question_text: To handle a hostile Point of Information, a debater should:
options: Stay calm, answer briefly or decline politely and continue the argument
